claims.text: The starting Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing material.
A critical combination of annealing temperature and time triggers intermetallic nucleation and growth.
The intermetallic compounds preferentially form at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary intermetallic formation occurs through partitioning of Mg and other solutes.
The intermetallic transformation directly correlates with a marked change in corrosion resistance.
The intermetallic transformation directly correlates with a marked change in high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Incremental annealing or aging while varying temperature and duration is the proposed intervention.
The range of approximately 700–900 °C overlaps relevant service conditions.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes partitioning of Mg and other solute elements.
Solute partitioning causes nucleation and coarsening of intermetallic compounds.
The resulting intermetallic phases disrupt or modify the continuity of protective surface oxides.
Modification of protective oxide continuity affects corrosion resistance.
Modification of protective oxide continuity affects high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Below the critical aging threshold, the alloy remains largely metastable.
Below the critical aging threshold, the alloy retains its initial protective properties.
Above the critical aging threshold, detectable intermetallic precipitation appears.
Intermetallic precipitation above the threshold is accompanied by a sudden, typically degrading change in corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic precipitation above the threshold is accompanied by a change in high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Intermetallic nucleation begins to become evident near approximately 700–900 °C.
The untreated comparison specimen is an as-milled metastable alloy.
